queue.title: Stop Lost-Time Injuries: PPE, Van Checks & Driving
queue.description:
Field safety starts long before you open the panel. In this HVAC School safety meeting, we lay out the everyday habits that keep technicians on the job and out of the hospital. We cover vehicle inspections, the right gloves, and staying alert behind the wheel. One theme runs through all of it: routine work becomes high-risk the moment you stop paying attention. The goal is to stop injuries before they turn into stitches, an OSHA recordable, or lost time away from work.

We open with a real story from the turnpike. A service van with low tire tread hydroplaned during a simple lane change, spun a full 360, and hit the wall. Luckily, nobody else was nearby. That near miss is why weekly van checks matter. Walk around your vehicle before you get in, check tire tread depth, have a coworker confirm your brake lights work, and report new noises right away through the QR code system. Dropping your van off for weekend maintenance catches worn brakes, leaks, and bald tires before they leave you stranded or worse.

Next, we talk about PPE, especially gloves. One of our techs had a hand sliced by sheet metal dangerously close to a main artery. Since then, we’ve challenged every technician to make gloves part of the daily routine. Skipping gloves for weeks without a problem tricks your brain into thinking it’s safe, until the day it isn’t. Today’s high-dexterity gloves let you feel screws, valves, and spade terminals, and welding sleeves protect your arms during brazing. Keep a spare pair clipped to your bag or belt so a rooftop gust of wind never catches you bare-handed.

We also cover driving. Distracted drivers, pedestrians glued to their phones, and electric scooters crossing intersections make every trip a risk. Use the Smith System, look left-right-left before crossing a crosswalk, and remember that dash cameras protect you if something goes wrong.

In the second half, we get into ladder safety, which is part of your van checks too. Secure ladders to the racks and racks to the vehicle, and replace sun-damaged straps. Never stand a short ladder on top of the van to reach a roof. When climbing, stay aware of anything bulky you’re carrying, like a backpack that can snag at the top or a drill that can fall on the person holding the ladder.

queue.title: EEV Diagnostics & Expansion Devices with Ty Branaman, Roman Baugh, & Bryan Orr
queue.description:
EEV diagnostics can be confusing, especially when a perfectly good valve looks bad on paper. In this HVAC School livestream, host Bryan Orr sits down with Ty Branaman and Roman Baugh for a deep dive into the electronic expansion valve: how it works, what it needs to do its job, and how to prove whether it has actually failed before you replace anything.

Ty starts with the evolution of expansion devices, from the fixed orifice (piston) and automatic expansion valve (AXV) to the TXV and finally the EEV, and explains what each metering device was designed to control. Roman then breaks down the stepper motor inside the valve, the difference between unipolar EEV and bipolar EEV designs, and how PID control logic lets mini split, inverter heat pump, VRF, and refrigeration systems modulate refrigerant flow far more precisely than a spring-operated TXV.

From there, the conversation moves into field troubleshooting: thermistor placement and sensor drift, pressure transducer readings, liquid line quality and subcooling, flash gas, and why there is no position feedback telling the board where the valve actually is. You’ll also hear practical tips on using a power cycle to overdrive valves closed, opening EEVs for nitrogen flow & evacuation, cleaning corrosion off the valve body, and using an EEV magnet or manual driver to test operation.

What We Cover:

Expansion Evolution: What problem is each expansion device family trying to solve?

Mechanical vs. Electronic: How an EEV’s stepper motor and control loop differ from a traditional TXV.

The “False Positive”: Which sensor or setup faults make a perfectly good valve look bad?

Mimicking Valve Failures: How low charge, liquid-line restrictions, flash gas, or lost pressure differentials disguise themselves as EEV issues.

Commanded Position: What step count actually proves, and what it doesn’t.

Pre-Replacement Protocol: Repeatable tests to run before condemning a valve, sensor, or board.

Live Q&A: Triaging real-world diagnostic scenarios from the audience.

Whether you’re chasing high superheat with a wide-open command, a suspected liquid line restriction, or a step count that doesn’t match what the system is doing, this HVAC troubleshooting session gives you a process to work from outside the valve in before reaching for a replacement. It’s useful HVAC training for anyone servicing modern inverter equipment.

queue.title: Glycol Skids for Market Refrigeration w/ Max Johnson
queue.description:
Glycol secondary loop systems are showing up in more and more grocery stores, and in this episode of the HVAC School Podcast, Bryan Orr sits down with Max, one of the company’s lead startup techs and its in-house subject matter expert on glycol skids. Max explains what these systems are, why clients are choosing them for retrofits, and what it takes to commission one without taking a live store down. The big picture: a traditional DX rack chills a water and propylene glycol mix in a heat exchanger, and that glycol is pumped around the store to cool the medium-temperature cases.

 The conversation starts with the “why.” Reduced refrigerant charge inside the building, keeping flammable or higher-GWP refrigerants out of the sales floor, regulatory pressure, and zero-emissions initiatives all push clients this way. Max is upfront that efficiency isn’t one of the reasons at this scale, since the extra heat exchange step, lower suction temperatures, and pump energy all cost something. He also covers the trade-off in reliability: case-level controls are simple, but a fault in one of the skid’s main valves can take out every case at once, so techs have to move fast.

 From there, Max walks through the skid itself, from the brazed plate heat exchanger, VFD-controlled pumps, and air separator to the expansion tank, strainers, suction guide, controller, and EEV drivers. He then covers flow control with balance valves, defrost strategy, and the importance of proper vents and drains in the piping. The two get into the details of startup and commissioning, and some key takeaways include pressure testing instead of pulling a vacuum, filling and purging air, and verifying that the refrigerant-side valves are wired and driven correctly so a swapped valve doesn’t flood the rack.

 The back half of the episode is practical field advice. Max shares how to recognize air in the loop, why store humidity and dew point matter so much for case performance, which specialty tools and fittings he carries, and how to handle glycol mixing and top-offs.

queue.title: How to Wire a Surge Protector to a Disconnect: Pigtails & Phasing Tape
queue.description:
Double lugging a surge protector onto the load-side terminals of a disconnect is common in the field, but it can get your install flagged on inspection. In this video, we show how to wire a surge protector to a disconnect the right way, with pigtails instead of a double lug, and why phasing tape on the white wire matters on 240V circuits.

Most disconnects and breakers aren’t rated for two conductors under one terminal. The wiring diagram for many surge protectors shows a double lug option, but that only applies when the terminals are listed for it. To keep the install code compliant, join the condenser wire and the surge protector lead with a wire nut and run a single jumper to each load-side terminal. That way there’s only one wire on each terminal. The same pigtail method applies when you wire a surge protector into a breaker panel.

We also cover phase identification. On a 240V circuit, the white conductor in the cable is being used as a hot, so code requires it to be marked. Wrap it with black or red phasing tape (or use a marker if you don’t have tape) so anyone opening the box knows it’s energized. If the existing wiring was never marked, take it off the terminal, tape it, and put it back, since you were the last one to touch it. On 120V circuits, leave the white wire alone, because it’s the neutral.

Other field tips in this video:

Picking the right wire nut size for the pigtail splice
Mounting the surge protector on the bottom or right side of the disconnect
Keeping the door hinge clear so the disconnect can still open and close
Taking a photo of every connection so you have a record if an inspector asks

These practices apply to ductless and mini split installs, split systems, new high-voltage runs to a condenser, and any surge protector wired at a disconnect or breaker.

queue.title: Your Thermostat Is Reading the Wall - Short #308
queue.description:
In this short podcast episode, Bryan talks about why your thermostat is reading the wall, not the actual air temperature.

 A thermostat is an instrument designed to read temperature (and sometimes humidity); it displays those readings based on sensors and makes decisions. Most of these sensors are thermistors, which are resistors that change resistance with changes in temperature. Thermistors have low mass and respond to radiant, convective, and conductive heat.

 Air coming through the wall (convective heat), the temperature of the things around the thermostat (radiant heat), AND the wall temperature (conductive heat) can influence your thermostat's reading. We may see a service call where the thermostat reads above the air temperature and runs the air conditioning unit even when the air temperature is already below the set point. Our first move as technicians should be to ask customers when they noticed the problem; the timing can give us some clues about what is going on. Looking behind the thermostat is one of the first things we should do, as air can move through the hole where wires come through, especially if there is air leakage elsewhere. If there is a temperature difference and an airflow path, that could be the source of the issue.  

 Use a reliable temperature probe near the thermostat, off the wall and away from the thermostat casing and electronics, to get a reliable temperature measurement to compare to the thermostat. If the probe and thermostat disagree after several minutes, we should investigate deeper for a warm wall. Infrared thermometers and thermal imagers can help you identify warm surfaces. Keep in mind that thermostats may have sensors in different locations, offsets, and programmed corrections as well. 

 If you find an open wire penetration, use non-flammable insulation and/or an appropriate putty to close it. Be careful not to block the sensing vents, too. Let everything settle and repeat the comparison. Some other solutions include changing the location of the thermostat or remote sensor.

queue.title: Next-Gen Filtration - Pressure Drop, MERV 16, and Bypass Prevention w/ Chris Howells
queue.description:
In this episode of the HVAC School Podcast, Bryan sits down with Chris Howells, senior training manager at AprilAire, to talk about what really makes a filtration system perform. Chris has nearly thirty years in the industry, including fifteen as a technician, and brings a field-first perspective on why filtration is more than just “a filter.” Bryan also admits up front that his own contracting company is looking to put more high-efficiency filters into the field, so this conversation doubles as a practical learning session.

 The discussion starts with a common misconception: that a “thicker” filter is simply a filter with thicker media. Chris explains that what matters is surface area, face velocity, and pressure drop, not the width of the cabinet. They cover why using the full face of the filter is one of the easiest wins, how a poorly designed return can load just one section of the media, and why a high MERV rating does not automatically mean high resistance. Cabinet design, media construction, and overall system design all play a role, and modern ECM blowers make low static pressure more important than ever.

 From there, the conversation turns to bypass air and measurement. Chris describes how AprilAire’s cabinets use top and bottom rails and a self-seal media overhang to force air through the filter, backed by a 10-year clean coil guarantee. He and Bryan stress using the right tools, including a dual-port manometer and a proper static pressure probe, and checking pre-filter and post-filter pressure drop against manufacturer performance data at around 500 feet per minute. Chris also debunks the idea that deeper media is always more restrictive, pointing out that a typical retail one-inch pleated filter can raise pressure drop dramatically compared with a basic fiberglass filter.

 The final stretch is about communication and growth. Chris and Bryan share simple, natural questions technicians can use to start air quality conversations without sounding like a sales pitch, and they encourage listeners to stay curious and keep asking “why.” Chris closes with resources for learning more, including AprilAirPartners.com and the AprilAire Academy, and mentions that the Santa Fe and UltraAire product lines are now part of the AprilAire family.

queue.title: Commercial Condensate Drain Leaking? Trap, Vent, and Slope Fix
queue.description:
Commercial condensate drain leaking and you can't figure out why? In this video, Jesus walks through a 10-ton commercial unit with a poorly built condensate drain. It has a shallow trap, a vent with no slope after it, and a drain pan that isn't seated correctly.

Commercial systems aren't like a quick residential install under the case. Drop ceilings, larger equipment, and higher static pressure mean you can't just throw in a couple of inches of drop and call it good. Jesus explains why you need to check static pressure first and find out whether the drain is under positive or negative pressure. On this positive-pressure system, a clean-out left wide open in place of a real trap pulls in air and the unit never drains properly. That leads to overflow and water leaking into the ceiling.

Then Jesus rebuilds the drain the right way:

Reseating the drain pan so it sits correctly
Sizing the trap from the manufacturer's manual instead of relying on rules of thumb
Installing a clean-out tee without letting it replace the trap
Making sure the vent sits higher than the drain pan
Running the drain line downhill at a quarter inch per foot of slope

If you're chasing callbacks on overflowing commercial units, this trap, vent, and slope fix is where to start.

queue.title: The Fuse Only Blows When You Leave - Short #307
queue.description:
In this short podcast episode, Bryan talks about the fuse that only blows when you leave. The service call usually goes like this: you replace a blown fuse, the system runs fine, you leave, and then the fuse blows again. There could be several causes of a blown fuse.

 First, ask what was happening right before the system stopped, such as if the unit was starting up, if it was raining outside, or if the operating mode changed. The customer may not know the specifics, but they may be able to offer a clue. If the control fuse blows during a specific call, we may be able to locate a short in one of the circuits involved. We may also be able to find out a bit by inspecting places where wire often gets damaged, such as common points where conductors pinch or rub.  

 Isolation diagnosis can help us isolate the specific circuit or component with a problem. First, look at the wiring diagram, label conductors, and take pictures of the original setup before disconnecting anything. Keep the correct fuse protection instead of using a larger fuse, leave all safety controls in the circuit, and use the manufacturer's test procedure if it's available. Then, isolate different loads and conductors so they can be energized individually; some modern thermostats make this easy. Also note that continuity testing alone isn't always reliable for locating problematic paths.

 Sometimes, motion (from motors), temperature, and moisture can also contribute to intermittent issues. Additionally, some inductive loads, like contactor coils, experience unique intermittent issues that cause the components to draw high current; inductive reactance matters. Measuring current on the different circuits as you energize them can also point you toward circuits that have higher current than expected.

 Once you've found and repaired something, go back to the condition that made it fail. Make sure you fix the underlying problem, such as exposure to excess heat, vibration, or moisture.

queue.title: Questionable CO Alarms w/ Bill Spohn
queue.description:
In this episode of the HVAC School Podcast, Bryan welcomes back Bill Spohn to talk about carbon monoxide and a troubling trend in the alarms being sold online. They start with the basics: the difference between a standard UL 2034 alarm and a true low-level CO monitor. UL 2034 alarms were designed to avoid nuisance calls, so they can stay silent through long exposures at relatively low concentrations. Low-level monitors are far more sensitive and can warn you that something is brewing before it becomes a life-threatening emergency.

 Bill explains why that gap matters, walking through how carbon monoxide displaces oxygen on hemoglobin, why it lingers in the body, and why children, older adults, and people with heart or lung conditions are especially vulnerable. Bryan adds the troubleshooting angle: a UL 2034 alarm is the safety net that keeps people from dying, but low-level monitoring helps you find and fix a problem early, much like catching a refrigerant leak before the system is flat.

 The conversation then turns to the main story. Bill bought a pair of inexpensive alarms advertised as both low-level and UL 2034 compliant, which is a contradiction, since the two cannot be the same device. They arrived with no instructions, no model number, and no visible certification control number, and they closely resembled a product tied to a Consumer Product Safety Commission warning covering roughly 375,000 units and 91 reported failures to alarm. Bill traces the marketing back to what appears to be a single factory selling under many brand names, backed by a virtual office address, a fake firefighter endorsement, and a flood of promotional emails.

 Bryan and Bill close with lessons for technicians, consumers, and manufacturers alike. Be skeptical when price and performance seem too good to be true, verify who is behind a brand, and remember that claiming to meet a standard is not the same as being independently certified. They also urge established manufacturers to be humble, test claims thoroughly, and make sure published specifications reflect how their sensors actually perform.

queue.title: Same Charge, Different Numbers - Short #306
queue.description:
In this short podcast episode, Bryan talks about what happens when you adjust the condenser airflow: you have the same charge, different numbers. This short covers HVAC condensers and flooded condensers in refrigeration applications.

 When you increase condenser airflow by repairing a condenser fan or washing the unit, the pressure and subcooling readings change even though the charge stays the same. Refrigerant enters the condenser as superheated vapor and goes through three stages: desuperheating, condensing, and subcooling. The key thing to remember is that these three stages can occur at different points of the condenser as the operating conditions change.

 Higher head pressure doesn't necessarily lead to higher subcooling, as subcooling depends on both saturation temperature and actual liquid temperature; if both change, head pressure can't tell us which way subcooling went. Exceptionally bad airflow across the condenser and high compression ratios can also interfere with liquid delivery. Uneven condenser airflow distribution also affects refrigerant distribution in the condenser. We shouldn't use low subcooling as an automatic indicator to add more charge.

 If there's one thing to remember, it's that you need to fix the airflow problem before deciding there is a charge problem. Operating readings can change without the total refrigerant charge changing.
